quick_notes.title: Early Associations
quick_notes.detail: Madras Native Association (1852 - Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty). Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884 - M. Veeraraghavachari, P. Anandacharlu).
quick_notes.explanation: The Madras Native Association was a political group formed in 1852 by a man named Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty. Its main goal was to ask the British government for fairer treatment of Indians, like lower taxes and more jobs in the administration. Later, in 1884, a new group called the Madras Mahajana Sabha was created by M. Veeraraghavachari and P. Anandacharlu. This Sabha, which means "assembly" or "society," was a more organized body that brought together educated Indians to discuss political issues and demand reforms. Both of these associations were early steps in the Indian freedom movement, showing how people in the Madras region (now part of Tamil Nadu) began to organize for their rights before the Indian National Congress was formed in 1885.

quick_notes.title: Subramania Bharati
quick_notes.detail: National Poet. Editor of "India" and "Vijaya". Composed "Swadesa Geethangal".
quick_notes.explanation: Subramania Bharati is a famous Tamil poet and writer, often called the National Poet of India because of his patriotic poems that inspired people

quick_notes.title: Vanchinathan
quick_notes.detail: Member of Bharatha Matha Association. Shot Collector Ashe at Maniyachi Junction (June 17, 1911) and committed suicide.
quick_notes.explanation: Vanchinathan was a revolutionary freedom fighter in India's struggle against British colonial rule. He was a member of the Bharatha Matha Association, a secret society that aimed to overthrow British control through armed resistance. On June 17, 1911, at Maniyachi Junction in present-day Tamil Nadu, Vanchinathan shot and killed Robert William d'Escourt Ashe, who was the District Collector of Tirunelveli. A Collector is a senior British official in charge of a district's administration and tax collection. After the killing, Vanchinathan committed suicide to avoid capture. This act was part of a larger plot to protest British policies and inspire other Indians to fight for independence.

quick_notes.title: Annie Besant & Home Rule
quick_notes.detail: Home Rule League in Madras (1916). Started "New India" and "Commonweal".
quick_notes.explanation: Annie Besant was a British woman who became a strong supporter of Indian self-rule. In 1916, she started the Home Rule League in Madras (now Chennai) to demand that India be allowed to govern itself within the British Empire, which is what "Home Rule" means. To spread her ideas, she launched two newspapers: "New India" and "Commonweal." "New India" was a daily newspaper that argued for Indian political rights, while "Commonweal" was a weekly paper that focused on social and political reform. Through these newspapers and her league, Besant helped build public support for the freedom movement, especially among people who had not yet joined the Indian National Congress. Her efforts made the demand for self-government a nationwide issue.
